name: Neo-Ottomanism
summary: Neo-Ottomanism is a Turkish current that seeks to reconcile the republic with its Ottoman, Islamic and multinational past and to use that heritage to make Turkey an active, self-confident power in the regions the empire once ruled: the Balkans, the Caucasus and the Middle East. Its defining scholarship describes it as favouring a moderate secularism with a larger public role for Islam, a less ethnic, more multicultural citizenship open to Kurdish cultural rights, a market economy, and soft power, trade and mediation abroad while keeping Turkey's NATO and EU ties. Its best-known statement, Ahmet Davutoglu's strategic depth doctrine and zero problems with neighbours policy, adds economic interdependence and support for democratic change, though Davutoglu himself rejects the neo-Ottoman label.
scope: As the defining scholarship sets it out: Taspinar (s5) defines neo-Ottomanism by three traits (coming to terms with the Ottoman and Islamic heritage with moderate secularism and Kurdish cultural rights; grandeur and soft power in former Ottoman lands; embracing the West as much as the Islamic world) and names Turgut Ozal as its early proponent and Davutoglu's strategic depth as its AKP-era form; Murinson (s6) and Carlucci and Ennas (s7) trace the same line from Ozal's circle (Cengiz Candar) to Davutoglu, and Grigoriadis (s8) discusses Davutoglu's doctrine as the one often called neo-Ottomanism. The profile answers from these accounts and from Davutoglu's own texts (s10-s12), which they tie to the ideology. Neo-Ottomanism was never the declared doctrine of the Turkish state (its main theorist rejects the label), so it has no state record of its own and every answer rests on words; AKP government practice, Erdogan's later militarised policy, pan-Turkism, Ottoman dynastic restorationism and the Gulen movement are other subjects.

notes: Rules-5 pass by claude-opus-5-5 (2026-11-09), brought up to the shared rules because the page gets search traffic. The first pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-16) rested mostly on two Wikipedia articles (s1, s4), a third-party copy of Davutoglu's 2008 essay (s2) and a Wilson Center profile (s3); under rules 5 Wikipedia is not evidence, so every first-pass answer was checked against the defining sources and changed or nulled (166 nulled), with the first version kept in each statement's reviewHistory. This pass read in full Taspinar's Carnegie paper (s5), Murinson's BESA monograph (s6), the neo-Ottoman sections of Carlucci and Ennas (s7), Grigoriadis's ELIAMEP paper (s8) and three texts by Davutoglu (s10-s12). Themes searched: world (alliances, EU, neighbours, Iraq, territorial claims), government (democracy, security and freedom, military tutelage, referenda), society and culture (Islam and secularism, headscarf, Kurdish rights, multiculturalism), economy (markets, trade). The defining sources say almost nothing on welfare, taxation, labour, family, sexuality, ecology or technology; those statements are null. Hristov's 2019 article in Social Evolution & History was read and left out (it rests on conspiracy claims about 'Anglo-Saxon and Jewish elites'); Insight Turkey and the Open University repository (Wastnidge 2019) refuse scripted access; Yavuz's Nostalgia for the Empire (2020) and Murinson's 2006 article are not open access. The old missing statement on former-empire influence now cites s5 and s7 instead of s1 and the third-party copy s2.
